title: Hand cleaning: when to do it and which product fits
audience: All cleaning and service staff who enter patient areas or handle equipment, linen and waste.
learningOutcomes: Name the five WHO hand hygiene moments as adopted in Australia.
Choose between an alcohol hand rub and soap with water for a given situation.
State the hand-care rules that keep hand hygiene effective.

instruction.heading: Why hands matter
instruction.body: Any organism that spreads by contact or by droplets can ride on the hands. Organisms may live on the hands at all times or be picked up during work, and they can pass from a patient to a surface and then to another patient. The guideline cites published studies in which better hand hygiene went with fewer infections caused by some antibiotic-resistant organisms. It is one control within a wider approach, not a stand-alone fix.

instruction.heading: The five moments
instruction.body: The five moments endorsed by the WHO and adopted in Australia identify when cleaning shields the patient from the worker's hands, the patient from their own organisms during invasive care, and the worker and setting from the patient's organisms. Clean on both sides of each patient encounter: on approach, before an aseptic task, after body-fluid exposure, after the encounter, and after touching the environment. A further cleaning follows glove removal.

instruction.heading: Non-clinical moments
instruction.body: Beyond direct care, hands need cleaning at shift start and finish, around meals, after toilet use, whenever visibly dirty, after handling laundry, equipment or waste, after nose or mouth contact, and after keyboard use in clinics. Outbreak periods add entries and exits from patient zones.

instruction.heading: Choosing the product
instruction.body: Alcohol-based rubs typically outperform ordinary or antiseptic soaps against common germs. They work well on many bacteria, mycobacteria and fungi, and reasonably on enveloped viruses. Certain viruses lacking an envelope, norovirus among them, respond less reliably, and Clostridium difficile spores survive exposure. Soap mechanically removes organisms, which is why it suits visibly grimy hands. If C. difficile or viruses lacking an envelope are of concern and no gloves were worn, scrub with soap and rinse, then dry carefully.

instruction.heading: Keeping the skin healthy
instruction.body: Cuts receive waterproof coverings. Keep nails trim and clean, avoid false nails, and steer clear of chipped varnish. Discourage watches and rings; a plain band may stay but should be turned while cleaning. Routine emollient keeps skin healthy and encourages steady practice. Individual facilities write their own jewellery and nail rules.

procedure: Work out whether the task you are about to do is a clinical or non-clinical moment.
Clean your hands before you touch the patient or anything around them.
Apply an alcohol rub to every surface of both hands and let it air-dry, as long as the hands are not visibly grubby.
If the hands are grubby or spores are a worry, wash with soap and running water, rinse and dry carefully.
Clean your hands again after removing gloves, after touching surroundings, and after any body-fluid exposure.
Put hand cream on when the shift ends and before breaks.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner has finished a bathroom where a C. difficile infection is known, and is about to enter the next patient's room.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What hand hygiene step should happen first?
workedExamples.reasoning: Take the gloves off, bin them and clean your hands right away. If the hands are grubby, or spores are the worry, wash with soap and running water and dry them. An alcohol rub on its own does not remove spores.

equipmentAndPpe: Alcohol hand rub with an approved product listing
Soap, running water and single-use towels

commonErrors.error: Using an alcohol rub on visibly dirty hands.
commonErrors.prevention: Dirty-looking hands call for a soap-and-water wash followed by thorough drying.

commonErrors.error: Relying on an alcohol rub when spores are the concern.
commonErrors.prevention: For spore or non-enveloped virus concerns, the guideline favours soap and running water.

commonErrors.error: Skipping hand cleaning after removing gloves.
commonErrors.prevention: Take gloves off, then clean hands at once.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Alcohol hand rubs are flammable. Keep them away from heat and open flame and store them as the label directs.
Choose an antiseptic-approved product listed by the Therapeutic Goods Administration that complies with the named test standard.
Notify the person who manages infection control or workplace health about any skin irritation, cracking or bleeding, and hold off on that product until advice arrives.

qualityStandard: Learner recites all five moments and cites a real example for each.
Learner chooses the correct product for visibly dirty hands and for a spore concern.
Learner cleans hands after glove removal without prompting.
documentationEvidence: Hand hygiene audit or self-check entry, where the facility requires one
Record of any skin reaction, reported to the supervisor
summary: Clean hands before and after patient contact, after glove removal, and at non-clinical moments.
Alcohol rubs suit most situations; soap and water suit visible dirt and spore concerns.
Keep nails short, avoid artificial nails, cover cuts, and use hand cream regularly.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of the five hand hygiene moments applies before a cleaner touches a patient's bedside table?
options: Only after the cleaning is finished and after the bins are emptied as well
Before handling the patient's surroundings, as one of the moments that protect the patient.
After touching the table, because it is no longer part of the patient's care.
Only as the shift winds down and after the staff room has been closed for the day

knowledgeChecks.question: When are soap and water preferred over an alcohol rub?
options: Whenever the hands look clean, after a long shift, before lunch, and at the end of each morning round
Visibly dirty hands, or a suspicion of spores or of viruses lacking an envelope, with no gloves worn.
Only when stock has run out and only if the sink is working and the water is warm enough to use
With gloves on, because soap works through the glove material and the gloves are then left on the bench

knowledgeChecks.question: What hand-care rule does the guideline give for artificial nails?
options: Artificial nails are recommended for protection and they are kept short and clean
Artificial nails are not worn, since they have been tied to higher organism loads.
Artificial nails are fine if they are painted with chip-resistant polish.
Artificial nails must be cleaned with bleach and worn with a glove on top

sourceReferences: Australian Guidelines for Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare, B1.1.1, B1.1.2 (5 moments, Table B1.1, Recommendation 1), B1.1.3 (products), B1.1.4 (other aspects), B1.1.5 (hand care); rights: not held by user; reworded (no copying)
Source priority: the NHMRC guideline is an official Australian source. Where it conflicts with informal or in-house cleaning advice, the guideline governs the points this lesson relies on.

Australian Guidelines for Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare, edition note: the 2019 edition is the current edition (NHMRC, https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-05/australian-guidelines-for-the-prevention-and-control-of-infection-in-healthcare.pdf; CONFIRMED in the figures register, checked 2026-11-02); the uploaded copy read on 2026-11-02 is the 2010 edition, so points taken from it are UNCONFIRMED against the 2019 text. The existing aged-care and medical-equipment lessons cite the 2019 edition.

Cross-checked against aged-care-infection-control-L04 and medical-equipment-cleaning-L04 (existing curriculum lessons): both place hand hygiene before and after patient surroundings, and after glove removal. The existing lessons do not state the alcohol versus soap rule, so that point is not cross-checked.
UNCONFIRMED: the EN1500 testing standard referenced by the Therapeutic Goods Administration, and its current edition.
